report.source_text: 8 months later, the patient presented at a private neurological practice due to recurrent diplopia accompanied by pain in his pelvis radiating to his right leg, urge incontinence and symptoms of a sensory polyneuropathy on his lower limbs. Furthermore, a left VIth cranial nerve palsy, decreased deep tendon reflexes, reduced sense of vibration and an unsteady gait were documented in the records.

report.source_text: A laboratory screening was conducted and revealed positive titres for a syphilis screening test. The diagnosis of syphilis was further confirmed by positive T. pallidum haemagglutination assay and serological activity with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) of 1:8.

report.source_text: After the diagnosis was confirmed, the patient received penicillin G 4 million International units (IU) intravenously six times per day for 14 days according to current guidelines.8 9 After an initial 4 days of inpatient intravenous therapy the patient was switched to an outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy via an antibiotic pump with pencillin G 24 million IU per day for the remaining days of the 14-day regimen. To additionally account for a possible need of a longer duration of treatment in later stages of infection (such as for late latent syphilis), one shot of long-acting Benzathine-Penicillin 2.4 million IU intramuscularly was added after the intravenous therapy.

report.source_text: 6 months after treatment, the patient did not notice any significant clinical amelioration. Visual acuity was still <20/200 on the right side and 20/100 on the left side. Also the ataxia had not changed. We were, however, able to demonstrate an improvement of the laboratory markers. In cerebrospinal fluid, mononuclear pleocytosis decreased from 93 to 12 cells/µL, protein levels decreased from 1.65 to 0.79 g/L and albumin decreased from 0.89 to 0.43 g/L. Furthermore, serological activity also decreased to a Treponema RPR of 1:2 after 9 months, which fulfils most current guidelines’ criteria for an adequate response to treatment (table 2).

report.source_text: On referral, the patient suffered from severe gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception and absent deep tendon reflexes. Furthermore, diminished pupillary reflex to light with preserved constriction during convergence, described as an Argyll-Robertson pupil as well as an almost complete loss of vision were found.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A married carpenter in his 60s initially presented to ophthalmology with 3 months of diplopia and was diagnosed with presumed congenital left IVth cranial nerve paresis with refractive errors. Eight months later, he developed progressive neurological symptoms including recurrent diplopia, pelvic pain radiating to the right leg, urge incontinence, and sensory polyneuropathy of the lower limbs. Neurological examination revealed left VIth cranial nerve palsy, decreased deep tendon reflexes, reduced vibration sense, and unsteady gait consistent with posterior column dysfunction. Four years after initial symptoms, on referral, he exhibited severe gait ataxia with diminished proprioception, absent deep tendon reflexes, Argyll-Robertson pupils (light-near dissociation), and almost complete vision loss. Laboratory evaluation confirmed active syphilis infection with positive screening tests, TPPA positivity, and RPR titer of 1:8. CSF analysis demonstrated neurosyphilis with mononuclear pleocytosis (93 cells/µL), elevated protein (1.65 g/L), elevated albumin, increased lactate, and intrathecal synthesis of IgG directed against T. pallidum. The patient received 14 days of high-dose intravenous penicillin G (4 million IU qid) via inpatient admission followed by outpatient antibiotic pump, plus intramuscular benzathine penicillin (2.4 million IU). Six months post-treatment, laboratory markers showed adequate response (CSF pleocytosis decreased to 12 cells/µL, protein decreased to 0.79 g/L, RPR decreased to 1:2 at 9 months), though clinical improvement was limited with persistent severe visual impairment and ataxia.
